proofs.proof_tex:
Let \(\mathscr E=\sigma(E_0)\).  Since \(z_0=\mathbb E_P[Z_j\mid E_0]\) is \(\mathscr E\)-measurable, adjoining \(z_0\) to the conditioning field generated by \(E_0\) does not change any of the following conditional expectations.  By \texttt{def:target} and linearity of conditional expectation,
\[
\tau_n(z_0)=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_s\left\{
\frac1{n_s}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}\mathbb E_P[B_{si}(1)\mid z_0,E_0]
-\frac1{n_s}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}\mathbb E_P[B_{si}(0)\mid z_0,E_0]
\right\}.
\tag{1}
\]
Assumption \texttt{ass:consistency} and the definition of \(\bar B_s^{\mathrm{obs}}\) imply
\[
\frac1{n_s}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}\mathbb E_P[B_{si}(1)\mid z_0,E_0]
=\mathbb E_P[\bar B_s^{\mathrm{obs}}\mid z_0,E_0].
\tag{2}
\]
Assumption \texttt{ass:event-transport} gives
\[
\frac1{n_s}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}\mathbb E_P[B_{si}(0)\mid z_0,E_0]
=m_s(z_{0s}).
\tag{3}
\]
Substitution of (2)--(3) into (1) proves the displayed identifying equality.  Assumption \texttt{ass:historical-regression} separately identifies \(m_s(x)\) as the observed-law conditional mean of an untreated pseudo-event response at \(X_{st}=x\).  Thus consistency and event transport prove the relationship between the causal target and the observed-law functional; that relationship is not imposed by definition.

Fix a successful cohort \(s\), abbreviate \(\bar B_s^{\mathrm{obs}}\) by \(\bar B_s\), and hold \(\gamma\in\mathbb R^{q_r}\) fixed.  The event part of the criterion in \texttt{def:fwl-regression} obeys the exact identity
\[
\frac1{n_s}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}
(B_{si}^{\mathrm{obs}}-\theta-e_0^\top\gamma)^2
=\frac1{n_s}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}(B_{si}^{\mathrm{obs}}-\bar B_s)^2
+(\bar B_s-\theta-e_0^\top\gamma)^2.
\tag{4}
\]
Consequently the unique minimizing event coefficient for fixed \(\gamma\) is
\[
\widehat\theta_s=\bar B_s^{\mathrm{obs}}-e_0^\top\gamma.
\tag{5}
\]
At (5) the event criterion is independent of \(\gamma\).  Apart from the first, constant term in (4), the profiled criterion is therefore
\[
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}
w_{st}\{Q_{sti}-b_r(u_{st})^\top\gamma\}^2,
\tag{6}
\]
which is exactly the historical weighted least-squares problem in \texttt{def:feasible-estimator}.  Passage of the normalized shape test implies \(L_s>0\) and \(G_s\succeq c_GL_sI_{q_r}\succ0\), so (6) has the unique minimizer \(\widehat\gamma_s\).  Hence
\[
\widehat\theta_s=\bar B_s^{\mathrm{obs}}-e_0^\top\widehat\gamma_s.
\tag{7}
\]
Using the definitions of \(\widehat m_s\), \(\theta_{\mathrm{FWL}}\), and \(\widehat\tau\) now yields, on every sample on which all selected fits exist,
\[
\theta_{\mathrm{FWL}}
=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_s
(\bar B_s^{\mathrm{obs}}-e_0^\top\widehat\gamma_s)
=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_s(\bar B_s^{\mathrm{obs}}-\widehat m_s)
=\widehat\tau.
\]

Fix a regular conditional experiment given \(E_0\), and write
\[
\mathscr X=\sigma\{X_{st}:1\le s\le S,\ 1\le t\le T\}.
\]
Choose the event path in a fixed compact subset of \(\mathcal Z_+\) lying in the interior of \(([0,1]^d)^S\).  All scalar response probabilities below are kept in a fixed interval \([\eta,1-\eta]\), with \(0<\eta<1/2\), and responses equal \(B\) times the corresponding Bernoulli variables.  The regression carriers and their perturbations are scaled inside the declared range and H\"older envelopes.  For \(p,p+v\in[\eta,1-\eta]\), two applications of the mean-value theorem to binary relative entropy give
\[
\operatorname{kl}(p+v,p)
\le \frac{v^2}{2\eta(1-\eta)}.
\tag{31}
\]

We first describe a causal completion common to all four channels.  Draw event outcomes independently of \(\mathscr X\).  Conditional on \(\mathscr X\), draw bounded historical response paths independently across \((s,i)\), from kernels that may vary with \((s,i)\) but satisfy
\[
\mathbb E_P[Q_{sti}\mid\mathscr X,E_0]=m_s(X_{st}).
\]
Then, with \(\varepsilon_{sti}=Q_{sti}-m_s(X_{st})\),
\[
\mathbb E_P[B_{si}^{\mathrm{obs}}\mid\mathscr X,E_0]
=\mathbb E_P[B_{si}^{\mathrm{obs}}\mid E_0],
\qquad
\mathbb E_P[\varepsilon_{sti}\mid\mathscr X,E_0]=0.
\tag{32}
\]
Complete the unobserved event-date untreated potential outcomes so that their cohort-average conditional means are \(m_s(z_{0s})\).  Set the observed and historical potential outcomes according to \texttt{ass:consistency} and \texttt{ass:historical-consistency}; make historical potential outcomes invariant to the event treatment and every potential outcome invariant to other units' assignments.  These choices verify limited anticipation, no spillovers, and event transport.  Set \(X_{st}^{\mathrm{obs}}=X_{st}\).  Conditional donor laws are chosen independently of the panel, identically over \(j\), with covariance and standardized fourth moment inside their stated envelopes.  Equation (32) verifies exactly the two restrictions defining \(\mathcal M_{N,T,\mathbf n}^{\dagger}(\lambda)\).  No identical response distribution or positive lower response variance is used.

For the treated channel, put
\[
V_{\mathrm{tr}}=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\frac{\pi_s^2}{n_s}=R_{\mathrm{tr}},
\qquad
v_s=c_0\frac{\pi_s}{n_sV_{\mathrm{tr}}^{1/2}}.
\]
Because \(V_{\mathrm{tr}}\ge\pi_s^2/n_s\), one has
\(|v_s|\le c_0n_s^{-1/2}\).  A sufficiently small fixed \(c_0>0\) therefore keeps all event-response probabilities in \([\eta,1-\eta]\).  Change only the treated event-response probability in cohort \(s\) by \(v_s\).  The untreated surface and every other observed law remain fixed.  Absorbing the fixed wealth scale into \(c_0\), the target separation and (31) give
\[
|\tau_{n,P_{1,\mathrm{tr}}}(z_0)-
\tau_{n,P_{0,\mathrm{tr}}}(z_0)|
=c_0V_{\mathrm{tr}}^{1/2},
\qquad
\operatorname{KL}(P_{1,\mathrm{tr}},P_{0,\mathrm{tr}})
\le C\sum_{s=1}^{S}n_sv_s^2\le Cc_0^2.
\tag{33}
\]

For the smoothing channel, choose \(s_*\) maximizing
\(\pi_s^2(Tn_s)^{-2\lambda/(2\lambda+d)}\), and let
\[
b=c_b(Tn_{s_*})^{-1/(2\lambda+d)},
\]
where the fixed \(c_b>0\) makes the bump support stay in the interior cube.  Perturb only that cohort by
\[
m_{s_*,1}(x)-m_{s_*,0}(x)
=c_1b^\lambda\psi((x-z_{0s_*})/b),
\tag{34}
\]
where \(\psi\) is a fixed compactly supported \(\lambda\)-H\"older bump with \(\psi(0)=1\).  Take as common carrier an affine function with a nonzero covariance-standardized gradient when \(\lambda>1\), and an asymmetric \(\lambda\)-cusp at the query when \(0<\lambda\le1\).  The carrier is chosen with fixed slack in the response-range, H\"older, and two-sided modulus bounds.  The increment of (34) over a displacement of size \(\delta\) is at most \(Cc_1\delta^\kappa\): for \(\delta\le b\) this is the scaled H\"older bound, and for \(\delta>b\) it follows from \(b^\lambda\le C\delta^\kappa\).  Hence a sufficiently small fixed \(c_1\) preserves both sides of the local-modulus condition.  Since \(S\) is fixed,
\[
\begin{aligned}
|\tau_{n,P_{1,\mathrm{sm}}}(z_0)-
\tau_{n,P_{0,\mathrm{sm}}}(z_0)|^2
&=c_1^2\pi_{s_*}^2b^{2\lambda}\\
&\ge c\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_s^2
(Tn_s)^{-2\lambda/(2\lambda+d)}
=cR_{\mathrm{sm}}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{35}
\]
Use an independent uniform historical design in this channel.  The probability of the bump support is at most \(Cb^d\).  Conditional product structure, (31), and integration over the design yield
\[
\operatorname{KL}(P_{1,\mathrm{sm}},P_{0,\mathrm{sm}})
\le CTn_{s_*}b^{2\lambda+d}\le C.
\tag{36}
\]

For the spacing channel, use the pair in \texttt{lem:geometric-mixing-spacing-obstruction}.  That pair has the declared marginal density bounds, design-only geometric mixing, full-design centering, and two-sided modulus, and it satisfies
\[
\int\min\{dP_{0,\mathrm{sp}},dP_{1,\mathrm{sp}}\}\ge a_{\mathrm{sp}}>0,
\qquad
|\tau_{n,P_{1,\mathrm{sp}}}(z_0)-
\tau_{n,P_{0,\mathrm{sp}}}(z_0)|^2
\ge cR_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}.
\tag{37}
\]
Only this positive affinity is used; no Kullback--Leibler bound is claimed for the spacing experiment.  The rare-active-block constant in that construction may be decreased while kept fixed in the sample sizes.  Its no-active-block probability then approaches one, whereas its target separation is merely multiplied by a positive fixed power of that constant.  Thus, when needed for confidence-interval lower bounds, the same construction has affinity larger than any prescribed number below one while retaining the order in (37).

For the donor channel, let \(D=Sd\), choose a cohort \(s_0\), choose a unit vector \(v_0\in\mathbb R^d\), and let \(v\in\mathbb R^D\) have block \(v_0\) in cohort \(s_0\) and zero in every other block.  Put
\[
z^{(1)}=z^{(0)}+c_2N^{-1/2}v,
\]
with \(c_2>0\) small enough that both centers remain in the fixed interior query region.  For \(\kappa=1\), choose the weighted regression carrier to have a nonzero linear slope in direction \(v\).  For \(0<\kappa=\lambda<1\), choose in cohort \(s_0\) the two-cusp carrier
\[
x\longmapsto c_3+c_4|v_0^\top(x-z_{s_0}^{(0)})|^\lambda
+c_5|v_0^\top(x-z_{s_0}^{(1)})|^\lambda,
\qquad c_4\ne c_5,
\tag{38}
\]
where \(c_4,c_5>0\) and \(c_4\ne c_5\).  Fixed rescaling keeps (38) in \([0,B]\) and in \(\mathcal H_d(\lambda,L)\).  At either center, moving outward along \(v_0\), away from the other center, makes both cusp increments have the same sign.  Ellipticity converts the standardized radius to Euclidean radius by fixed factors.  Hence (38) satisfies the lower and upper local-modulus inequalities at both centers for every \(0<\delta\le\delta_0\).  Moreover, the unequal cusp coefficients give
\[
\left|\sum_s\pi_s
\{m_s(z_s^{(1)})-m_s(z_s^{(0)})\}\right|
\ge cN^{-\kappa/2}.
\tag{39}
\]

To construct the donor observations, take a common finite support in \(\mathbb R^D\) whose affine span is \(\mathbb R^D\), with all baseline atom probabilities in the interior of the simplex and covariance strictly inside the ellipticity envelope.  The linear map from probability perturbations of total mass zero to mean perturbations is onto because of the affine-span condition.  Thus there is a bounded probability score shifting the mean from \(z^{(0)}\) to \(z^{(1)}\).  For small \(c_2\) all probabilities remain positive; covariance and standardized fourth moment stay within their envelopes by continuity.  Taylor expansion of the finite probability-vector likelihood on this compact simplex neighborhood gives
\[
\operatorname{KL}(P_{1,\mathrm{don}},P_{0,\mathrm{don}})
\le CN\|z^{(1)}-z^{(0)}\|_2^2\le Cc_2^2.
\tag{40}
\]
Keep the historical observed law, its common surface, and the observed event mean fixed across the two donor laws.  Complete the unobserved untreated event outcomes under law \(\ell\) with cohort means \(m_s(z_s^{(\ell)})\).  The identifying equality in \texttt{lem:identification-fwl} turns (39) into a target separation whose square is at least \(cN^{-\kappa}=cR_{\mathrm{don}}\).

It remains to check affinity in the three bounded-divergence channels.  For any two laws, data processing under the event \(A=\{dP_1/dP_0\ge1\}\), followed by twice differentiating binary relative entropy, gives
\[
\operatorname{KL}(P_1,P_0)
\ge2\|P_1-P_0\|_{\mathrm{TV}}^2,
\qquad
\int\min\{dP_0,dP_1\}
=1-\|P_1-P_0\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\ge1-\sqrt{\operatorname{KL}(P_1,P_0)/2}.
\tag{41}
\]
Reducing \(c_0,c_1,c_2\) makes (41) uniformly positive for the treated, smoothing, and donor pairs; (37) supplies affinity directly for spacing.  The query is in \(\mathcal Z_+\) with conditional probability one, hence at least \(c_X\).  The causal completion preceding (31), together with the channelwise support, design, smoothness, donor, and modulus checks, proves that all four pairs belong to the same class \(\mathcal M_{N,T,\mathbf n}^{\dagger}(\lambda)\) and proves every assertion.

For a channel \(q\), take \((P_{0,q},P_{1,q})\) from \texttt{lem:joint-law-embedding}, write their conditional target values as \(\theta_0,\theta_1\), and put \(\Delta_q=|\theta_1-\theta_0|\).  Their conditional testing affinity is at least a fixed \(a_0>0\), and \(\Delta_q^2\ge cR_q\).  For any observed-data estimator \(\widetilde\tau\), the events
\[
E'_0=\{|\widetilde\tau-\theta_0|\ge\Delta_q/2\},
\qquad
E'_1=\{|\widetilde\tau-\theta_1|\ge\Delta_q/2\}
\]
cover the sample space.  Integration against the overlap measure therefore gives
\[
P_{0,q}(E'_0\mid E_0)+P_{1,q}(E'_1\mid E_0)\ge a_0,
\]
and hence
\[
\max_{\ell\in\{0,1\}}
\mathbb E_{P_{\ell,q}}
[(\widetilde\tau-\theta_\ell)^2\mid E_0]
\ge\frac{a_0\Delta_q^2}{8}\ge cR_q.
\tag{42}
\]
Maximizing over the four channels, using \(R_{\star,\beta}=\max_qR_q\), and then taking the supremum over \(\mathcal M_{N,T,\mathbf n}^{\dagger}(\lambda)\) and infimum over estimators proves the minimax lower bound.

For the upper bound let
\[
\mathscr X=\sigma\{X_{st}:s\le S,\ t\le T\},
\]
and condition on \((\mathscr X,E_0,(Z_j)_{j=1}^{N})\).  On the event of successful fits, \texttt{lem:identification-fwl} and the linear representation in \texttt{def:honest-interval} give
\[
\widehat\tau-\tau_n(z_0)
=U_{\mathrm{evt}}-U_{\mathrm{hist}}-B_{\mathrm{LP}}-B_{\mathrm{don}},
\tag{43}
\]
where
\[
U_{\mathrm{evt}}=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}\frac{\pi_s}{n_s}
\{B_{si}^{\mathrm{obs}}-\mathbb E_P[B_{si}^{\mathrm{obs}}\mid E_0]\},
\]
\[
U_{\mathrm{hist}}=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}\pi_s
\sum_{t=1}^{T}a_{sti}\varepsilon_{sti},
\]
\[
B_{\mathrm{LP}}=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_s
\left\{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}a_{sti}m_s(X_{st})
-m_s(\widetilde z_s)\right\},
\]
\[
B_{\mathrm{don}}=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_s
\{m_s(\widetilde z_s)-m_s(z_{0s})\}.
\]
The two full-design restrictions center the first two sums under the displayed conditioning; donor independence permits the donor sample to be adjoined.  Conditional cross-unit independence and the response range bound imply
\[
\mathbb E_P[U_{\mathrm{evt}}^2\mid\mathscr X,E_0,(Z_j)]
\le B^2\sum_{s=1}^{S}\frac{\pi_s^2}{n_s}=B^2R_{\mathrm{tr}}.
\tag{44}
\]
Treating the entire response history of one unit as one cluster, \texttt{lem:full-data-local-polynomial-control} similarly gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_P[U_{\mathrm{hist}}^2\mid\mathscr X,E_0,(Z_j)]
&\le B^2\sum_{s=1}^{S}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}
\left[\pi_s\sum_t|a_{sti}|\right]^2\\
&\le B^2c_G^{-1}R_{\mathrm{tr}}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{45}
\]
No temporal outcome restriction and no identical response law is used in (45).

Let \(C_K\) bound the Euclidean radius of the support of \(K\).  Whenever \(w_{st}>0\),
\(\|X_{st}-\widetilde z_s\|_2\le C_Kh_s\).  Polynomial reproduction, the H\"older Taylor remainder, and the deterministic absolute-weight bound give
\[
|B_{\mathrm{LP}}|\le C\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_sh_s^\lambda.
\tag{46}
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\((\sum_s\pi_sh_s^\lambda)^2\le S\sum_s\pi_s^2h_s^{2\lambda}\).  Apply \texttt{lem:geometric-mixing-selector-control} with exponent \(2\lambda\), conditionally on \(\widetilde z_s\), and then integrate over the donor sample.  Because \(S\) and the positive weights are fixed,
\[
\mathbb E_P[B_{\mathrm{LP}}^2\mathbf1_{\mathrm{good}}\mid E_0]
\le C\{R_{\mathrm{sm}}+R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}+N^{-\lambda}\}
\le CR_{\star,\beta},
\tag{47}
\]
where \(N^{-\lambda}\le N^{-\kappa}\) follows from \(\kappa=\min\{\lambda,1\}\).

Put \(D=Sd\) and define the proof variables
\[
Y_j=\Sigma^{-1/2}(Z_j-z_0),
\qquad
W_N=N^{-1/2}\sum_{j=1}^{N}Y_j.
\]
Donor replication gives conditionally independent mean-zero vectors with
\(\mathbb E_P[Y_jY_j^\top\mid E_0]=I_D\).  On expanding \(\|W_N\|_2^4\), every term containing a singleton sample index has conditional expectation zero.  The all-equal terms and the three pairings give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_P[\|W_N\|_2^4\mid E_0]
&=\frac1N\mathbb E_P[\|Y_1\|_2^4\mid E_0]\\
&\quad+\left(1-\frac1N\right)
\{(\operatorname{tr}I_D)^2+2\operatorname{tr}(I_D^2)\}\\
&\le\frac BN+\left(1-\frac1N\right)(D^2+2D)=M_4(N).
\end{aligned}
\tag{48}
\]
Consequently
\[
\mathbb E_P[\|\Sigma^{-1/2}(\bar Z-z_0)\|_2^4\mid E_0]
\le CN^{-2}.
\tag{49}
\]
Euclidean projection onto the cube cannot increase distance from \(z_0\), and the covariance eigenvalue bounds imply
\[
\|\Sigma^{-1/2}(\widetilde z-z_0)\|_2
\le\sqrt{C_\Sigma/c_\Sigma}\,
\|\Sigma^{-1/2}(\bar Z-z_0)\|_2.
\tag{50}
\]
On the event where the left side of (50) is at most \(\delta_0\), the upper local-modulus inequality bounds \(|B_{\mathrm{don}}|^2\) by a fixed constant times that norm to the power \(2\kappa\).  Lyapunov's inequality and (49) bound its expectation by \(CN^{-\kappa}\).  On the complementary event, boundedness gives \(|B_{\mathrm{don}}|\le B\), while Markov's inequality and (49) make the event probability \(O(N^{-2})\).  Since \(0<\kappa\le1\),
\[
\mathbb E_P[B_{\mathrm{don}}^2\mid E_0]
\le CN^{-\kappa}=CR_{\mathrm{don}}.
\tag{51}
\]

Every successful intercept satisfies
\[
|\widehat m_s|\le B\sum_{t,i}|a_{sti}|\le Bc_G^{-1/2},
\]
and a failed intercept contribution is zero.  Thus the squared estimation error is uniformly bounded on the bad sample.  The bad-sample probability bound in \texttt{lem:geometric-mixing-selector-control} makes that contribution at most \(CR_{\star,\beta}\) along the asserted arrays.  Combining (43)--(51) with
\((x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4)^2\le4\sum_{j=1}^{4}x_j^2\) proves
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal M_{N,T,\mathbf n}^{\dagger}(\lambda)}
\mathbb E_P[(\widehat\tau-\tau_n(z_0))^2\mid E_0]
\le CR_{\star,\beta}.
\tag{52}
\]
The same quantity upper-bounds the minimax infimum because \(\widehat\tau\) is one observed-data estimator, independent of the unknown \(\Sigma\).

For completeness, set \(a=2\lambda/(2\lambda+d)\).  For every integer \(T\ge3\), weighted arithmetic--geometric mean and \(\log T\ge1\) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
(Tn_s)^{-2\lambda/(2\lambda+d)}
&=(n_s^{-1})^a(T^{-2\lambda/d})^{1-a}\\
&\le an_s^{-1}+(1-a)R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}.
\end{aligned}
\]
After multiplying by \(\pi_s^2\), summing, and using \(\sum_s\pi_s^2\le1\),
\[
R_{\mathrm{sm}}
\le aR_{\mathrm{tr}}+(1-a)R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}
\le R_{\mathrm{tr}}\vee R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}.
\tag{53}
\]
Thus
\[
R_{\star,\beta}=R_{\mathrm{tr}}\vee R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}\vee R_{\mathrm{don}}
\qquad(T\ge3).
\]
Equations (42) and (52) establish the same-class bracket in every relative-growth regime.  The full donor covariance enters through the standardized modulus and (50), but neither the estimator nor the proof estimates it.

Let
\[
\mathscr X=\sigma\{X_{st}:s\le S,\ t\le T\},
\]
and condition first on \((\mathscr X,E_0,(Z_j)_{j=1}^{N})\).  On each successful fit, polynomial reproduction from \texttt{lem:full-data-local-polynomial-control}, applied to the degree-\(r\) Taylor polynomial of \(m_s\) at \(\widetilde z_s\), gives
\[
\left|e_0^\top\widehat\gamma_s-m_s(\widetilde z_s)
-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}a_{sti}\varepsilon_{sti}\right|
\le C_{r,d}L\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}|a_{sti}|
\|X_{st}-\widetilde z_s\|_2^\lambda.
\tag{54}
\]
After cohort weighting, the right side of (54) is exactly \(A_L\).

Define the historical unit-cluster variables
\[
U_{si}=\pi_s\sum_{t=1}^{T}a_{sti}\varepsilon_{sti}.
\]
Assumption \texttt{ass:historical-full-design-centering} gives
\[
\mathbb E_P[U_{si}\mid\mathscr X,E_0,(Z_j)]=0;
\]
donor independence permits the donor sample to be added to the conditioning field.  Assumption \texttt{ass:cross-unit-independence} makes the \(U_{si}\)'s independent over \((s,i)\) under that conditioning.  Since \(0\le Q_{sti}\le B\), the conditional range length of \(U_{si}\) is at most
\[
c_{si}=B\pi_s\sum_{t=1}^{T}|a_{sti}|.
\]
If a conditionally centered random variable \(U\) lies in an interval of length \(c\), convexity of \(x\mapsto e^{vx}\) bounds its conditional exponential moment by the endpoint mixture with the same mean.  Direct differentiation of the logarithm of that mixture gives
\[
\mathbb E[e^{vU}\mid\mathscr X,E_0,(Z_j)]\le e^{v^2c^2/8}.
\tag{55}
\]
Multiplying (55) over independent unit clusters, applying the exponential Markov inequality, optimizing over \(v>0\), and repeating for \(-U\) yield
\[
P_P\left\{
\left|\sum_{s=1}^{S}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}U_{si}\right|>R_{\mathrm{hist}}
\,\middle|\,\mathscr X,E_0,(Z_j)\right\}
\le\alpha_{\mathrm{hist}}.
\tag{56}
\]
This treats each unit's entire calendar history as one bounded cluster and uses no within-unit temporal independence or mixing.

Similarly define
\[
V_{si}=\frac{\pi_s}{n_s}
\{B_{si}^{\mathrm{obs}}-\mathbb E_P[B_{si}^{\mathrm{obs}}\mid E_0]\}.
\]
Assumption \texttt{ass:event-full-design-mean-stability} centers \(V_{si}\) given \((\mathscr X,E_0)\); donor independence preserves that centering after the donors are adjoined, and cross-unit independence makes the variables conditionally independent.  Their conditional range lengths are at most \(B\pi_s/n_s\).  The same calculation gives
\[
P_P\left\{
\left|\sum_{s=1}^{S}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}V_{si}\right|>R_{\mathrm{evt}}
\,\middle|\,\mathscr X,E_0,(Z_j)\right\}
\le\alpha_{\mathrm{evt}}.
\tag{57}
\]
A union bound combines (56)--(57), so no independence between a unit's historical path and its event outcome is required.

For donor calibration define only for this proof
\[
Y_j=\Sigma^{-1/2}(Z_j-z_0),
\qquad
W_N=N^{-1/2}\sum_{j=1}^{N}Y_j.
\]
Conditional iid donor replication gives
\(\mathbb E_P[Y_j\mid E_0]=0\) and
\(\mathbb E_P[Y_jY_j^\top\mid E_0]=I_D\), where \(D=Sd\).  Expanding the fourth power, terms containing a singleton sample index vanish.  The all-equal and three paired index patterns give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_P[\|W_N\|_2^4\mid E_0]
&=\frac1N\mathbb E_P[\|Y_1\|_2^4\mid E_0]\\
&\quad+\left(1-\frac1N\right)
\{(\operatorname{tr}I_D)^2+2\operatorname{tr}(I_D^2)\}\\
&\le\frac BN+\left(1-\frac1N\right)(D^2+2D)
=M_4(N).
\end{aligned}
\tag{58}
\]
Define the proof event
\[
\mathcal D_N=\{\|W_N\|_2\le q_N\}.
\]
Markov's inequality and the definition of \(q_N\) imply
\[
P_P(\mathcal D_N^c\mid E_0)
\le\frac{M_4(N)}{q_N^4}=\alpha_{\mathrm{don}}.
\tag{59}
\]
Coordinatewise projection onto \([0,1]^{Sd}\) cannot increase Euclidean distance from \(z_0\), because \(z_0\) belongs to that cube.  The covariance eigenvalue bounds consequently give, on \(\mathcal D_N\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|\Sigma^{-1/2}(\widetilde z-z_0)\|_2
&\le c_\Sigma^{-1/2}\|\widetilde z-z_0\|_2\\
&\le c_\Sigma^{-1/2}\|\bar Z-z_0\|_2\\
&\le\sqrt{C_\Sigma/c_\Sigma}\,q_N/\sqrt N
=\delta_N.
\end{aligned}
\tag{60}
\]
On the good event in \texttt{def:honest-interval}, \(\delta_N\le\delta_0\).  The upper half of \texttt{ass:local-two-sided-modulus} and (60) then imply
\[
\left|\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_s
\{m_s(\widetilde z_s)-m_s(z_{0s})\}\right|
\le C_{\mathrm{mod}}\delta_N^\kappa=A_{\mathrm{don}}.
\tag{61}
\]

Let \(\mathcal G\) denote the selector-and-radius good event in \texttt{def:honest-interval}; it is measurable with respect to \((\mathscr X,E_0,(Z_j))\).  On \(\mathcal G^c\), the fallback interval is \([-B,B]\).  Each potential-outcome contrast has conditional mean in \([-B,B]\), and the positive cohort weights sum to one, so \(\tau_n(z_0)\in[-B,B]\) deterministically.  On \(\mathcal G\cap\mathcal D_N\), the identification equality, (54), and (61) decompose the estimator error into the event fluctuation, the historical fluctuation, and two terms bounded by \(A_L\) and \(A_{\mathrm{don}}\).  Hence noncoverage implies failure of (56) or (57).  Iterated conditioning gives, for every positive \(N,T,n_1,\ldots,n_S\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_P\{\tau_n(z_0)\notin C_\alpha\mid E_0\}
&\le P_P(\mathcal D_N^c\mid E_0)\\
&\quad+\mathbb E_P\!\left[
\mathbf1_{\mathcal G\cap\mathcal D_N}
P_P\{\text{historical failure or event failure}
\mid\mathscr X,E_0,(Z_j)\}
\,\middle|\,E_0\right]\\
&\le\alpha_{\mathrm{don}}+\alpha_{\mathrm{hist}}
+\alpha_{\mathrm{evt}}=\alpha.
\end{aligned}
\tag{62}
\]
No selector-tail probability is used for (62), so the coverage conclusion is finite-sample and exact.

For expected length, \texttt{lem:full-data-local-polynomial-control} gives deterministically on a successful fit
\[
R_{\mathrm{hist}}
\le B\left\{\frac12\log(2/\alpha_{\mathrm{hist}})c_G^{-1}
R_{\mathrm{tr}}\right\}^{1/2},
\qquad
R_{\mathrm{evt}}
=B\left\{\frac12\log(2/\alpha_{\mathrm{evt}})
R_{\mathrm{tr}}\right\}^{1/2}.
\tag{63}
\]
The support of \(K\) and the same deterministic weight bound give
\[
A_L\le C\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_sh_s^\lambda.
\]
Apply \texttt{lem:geometric-mixing-selector-control} with exponent \(\lambda\), conditionally on the projected donor center, and use Cauchy--Schwarz across the fixed cohorts.  This gives
\[
\sup_P\mathbb E_P[A_L\mathbf1_{\mathcal G}\mid E_0]
\le C\{R_{\mathrm{sm}}^{1/2}
+R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}^{1/2}+N^{-\lambda/2}\}
\le CR_{\star,\beta}^{1/2}.
\tag{64}
\]
Since \(D\) and \(\alpha\) are fixed, (58) implies \(q_N\le C\), whence
\[
A_{\mathrm{don}}\le CN^{-\kappa/2}=CR_{\mathrm{don}}^{1/2}.
\tag{65}
\]
The selector lemma gives
\(P_P(\mathcal G^c\mid E_0)\le CR_{\star,\beta}\) along the stated arrays.  The fallback length is at most \(2B\), and eventually \(R_{\star,\beta}\le R_{\star,\beta}^{1/2}\).  Since
\(\operatorname{length}(C_\alpha)\le2H_\alpha\) on \(\mathcal G\), (63)--(65) prove
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal M_{N,T,\mathbf n}^{\dagger}(\lambda)}
\mathbb E_P[\operatorname{length}(C_\alpha)\mid E_0]
\le C_\alpha^{\mathrm{up}}R_{\star,\beta}^{1/2}.
\tag{66}
\]

For the matching lower bound, choose the fixed perturbation constants in \texttt{lem:joint-law-embedding} so that every channel affinity \(A_q\) exceeds \(2\alpha+a_0\) for some fixed \(a_0>0\).  This is possible for the three Kullback--Leibler-controlled channels by taking their fixed perturbation constants sufficiently small and using (41) of that lemma's proof; it is possible for the spacing channel by the adjustable rare-block constant described there.  These choices change only positive constants in the target separations.  Let \(I\) be finite-sample conditionally honest, let \(\theta_0,\theta_1\) be a channel pair's target values, and let \(\mu_q=P_{0,q}\wedge P_{1,q}\) be the conditional overlap measure.  Uniform conditional honesty and domination by the two laws imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mu_q\{\theta_0,\theta_1\in I\}
&\ge\mu_q(\Omega)
-P_{0,q}\{\theta_0\notin I\mid E_0\}
-P_{1,q}\{\theta_1\notin I\mid E_0\}\\
&\ge A_q-2\alpha\ge a_0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{67}
\]
On this event, \(\operatorname{length}(I)\ge|\theta_1-\theta_0|\).  Therefore
\[
\max_{\ell\in\{0,1\}}
\mathbb E_{P_{\ell,q}}[\operatorname{length}(I)\mid E_0]
\ge a_0|\theta_1-\theta_0|
\ge c_\alpha R_q^{1/2}.
\tag{68}
\]
Maximizing (68) over the four channels gives the lower bound
\(c_\alpha R_{\star,\beta}^{1/2}\).  If an interval sequence is only uniformly asymptotically conditionally honest, then for every \(\epsilon>0\) both noncoverage probabilities are eventually at most \(\alpha+\epsilon\).  Taking \(\epsilon<a_0/4\) replaces the last lower bound in (67) by \(a_0-2\epsilon\ge a_0/2\), proving the same rate.  Equations (62), (66), and (68) establish all assertions.

Under the first specialization, \(S=1\) and \(\sum_s\pi_s=1\) imply \(\pi_1=1\).  The identifying equality in \texttt{lem:identification-fwl} and the restriction \(m_1(x)=x+\Delta_0\) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\tau_n(z_0)
&=\mathbb E_P[\bar B_1^{\mathrm{obs}}\mid z_0,E_0]-m_1(z_{01})\\
&=\mathbb E_P[\bar B_1^{\mathrm{obs}}\mid z_0,E_0]-z_{01}-\Delta_0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{69}
\]
When the scalar proxy is the event cohort's baseline outcome, \(z_{01}\) is its conditional baseline mean.  When \(\Delta_0\) is the untreated cohort-average post-minus-baseline mean change, (69) is treated post minus treated baseline minus the untreated post-minus-baseline change.  This is precisely the canonical conditional finite-cohort two-period difference-in-differences contrast.

For the second specialization define the cohort effect
\[
\tau_s=\frac1{n_s}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}
\mathbb E_P[B_{si}(1)-B_{si}(0)\mid z_0,E_0].
\]
Homogeneity across cohorts states that \(\tau_s=\tau^{\mathrm{com}}\) for every \(s\).  By \texttt{def:target} and \(\sum_s\pi_s=1\),
\[
\tau_n(z_0)=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_s\tau_s
=\tau^{\mathrm{com}}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_s
=\tau^{\mathrm{com}}.
\tag{70}
\]
The stipulated absence of carry-over beyond \(h=0\) makes this common terminal-level contrast the contemporaneous finite-cohort treatment effect on the level-wealth path defined in \texttt{def:buyhold-level}.  That final causal interpretation uses the stated specialization; it does not follow from the aggregation algebra alone.

Fix a successful cohort and suppress its index.  Write \(\mathsf L=L_s\), \(G=G_s\), and
\[
v_{ti}=w_{st}^{1/2}b_r(u_{st}).
\]
Then
\[
G=\sum_{t,i}v_{ti}v_{ti}^\top,
\qquad
a_{sti}=w_{st}^{1/2}e_0^\top G^{-1}v_{ti}.
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz and the definition of \(G\) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{t,i}|a_{sti}|
&\le
\left\{\sum_{t,i}(e_0^\top G^{-1}v_{ti})^2\right\}^{1/2}
\left\{\sum_{t,i}w_{st}\right\}^{1/2}\\
&=\{e_0^\top G^{-1}GG^{-1}e_0\}^{1/2}\mathsf L^{1/2}
=\{\mathsf Le_0^\top G^{-1}e_0\}^{1/2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]
The selector requires \(G/\mathsf L\succeq c_GI_{q_r}\).  Thus
\(G^{-1}\preceq(c_G\mathsf L)^{-1}I_{q_r}\).  Under the declared monomial normalization, \(e_0=b_r(0)\) is the constant-monomial coordinate and \(\|e_0\|_2=1\), whence
\[
\mathsf Le_0^\top G^{-1}e_0\le c_G^{-1}.
\tag{9}
\]
This proves the first displayed chain in the claim.

For fixed \((s,t)\), neither \(u_{st}\) nor \(w_{st}\) depends on the replicated-unit index, and
\[
G_s=n_s\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{st}b_r(u_{st})b_r(u_{st})^\top.
\]
Thus \(a_{sti}\) is constant in \(i\).  Equations (8)--(9) consequently imply
\[
\sum_t|a_{sti}|\le\frac{c_G^{-1/2}}{n_s}.
\tag{10}
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{s=1}^{S}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}
\left[\pi_s\sum_t|a_{sti}|\right]^2
&\le\sum_{s=1}^{S}n_s
\left(\frac{\pi_sc_G^{-1/2}}{n_s}\right)^2\\
&=c_G^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\frac{\pi_s^2}{n_s}
=c_G^{-1}R_{\mathrm{tr}}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]

It remains to verify the bias claim.  The normal equations and invertibility of \(G_s\) reproduce every polynomial \(p\) of total degree at most \(r\):
\[
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}a_{sti}p(u_{st})=p(0).
\tag{12}
\]
Indeed, writing \(p(u)=c^\top b_r(u)\), the left side equals
\(e_0^\top G_s^{-1}G_sc=e_0^\top c=p(0)\).  Subtract the degree-\(r\) Taylor polynomial of \(m_s\) at \(\widetilde z_s\).  The remainder convention in \texttt{ass:holder-smoothness}, with \(r=\lceil\lambda\rceil-1\), gives
\[
|m_s(x)-T_{r,\widetilde z_s}m_s(x)|
\le C_{r,d}L\|x-\widetilde z_s\|_2^\lambda.
\tag{13}
\]
Multiplication by \(|a_{sti}|\), summation over \((t,i)\), and then weighting by \(\pi_s\) bounds the absolute aggregate Taylor remainder by
\[
C_{r,d}L\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_s
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}|a_{sti}|
\|X_{st}-\widetilde z_s\|_2^\lambda=A_L.
\]
Every step is deterministic on a successful fit, and no upper bound on \(L_s\) has been used.

Condition throughout on \((E_0,\widetilde z_s=z)\).  By \texttt{ass:donor-independence}, adjoining \(\widetilde z_s\), which is a measurable function of the donor sample and \(E_0\), does not alter the conditional law of the historical design.  By \texttt{ass:temporal-mixing}, the stacked design process alone obeys the geometric absolute-regularity bound; no restriction on a historical outcome path is used below.

For \(z\in[0,1]^d\) and \(0<h\le1\), define
\[
\ell_{z,h}(x)=K((x-z)/h),
\qquad
\Phi_{z,h}(x)=K((x-z)/h)b_r((x-z)/h)b_r((x-z)/h)^\top.
\]
Bounded support of \(K\), the upper density bound, and the change of variables \(x=z+hu\) give a constant \(C_0<\infty\) such that
\[
\mathbb E_P[\ell_{z,h}(X_{st})\mid E_0]\le C_0h^d.
\tag{14}
\]
There is also a uniform lower bound.  Choose \(\eta>0\) and \(k_0>0\) such that \(K(u)\ge k_0\) on \([ -\eta,\eta]^d\).  For every \(z\) the rescaled intersection \(h^{-1}([0,1]^d-z)\) contains one member of a fixed finite collection of orthant boxes having positive side length.  On any such box a nonzero polynomial \(v^\top b_r(u)\) cannot vanish almost everywhere.  Compactness of the unit sphere in the fixed-dimensional space \(\mathbb R^{q_r}\), followed by the lower density bound, therefore gives \(c_0>0\) such that, uniformly in \(s,t,z,h\),
\[
c_0h^d\le\mathbb E_P[\ell_{z,h}(X_{st})\mid E_0],
\qquad
\mathbb E_P[v^\top\Phi_{z,h}(X_{st})v\mid E_0]
\ge c_0h^d\|v\|_2^2.
\tag{15}
\]
Fix the procedural threshold so that \(0<c_G<c_0/(4C_0)\).

Let \(A_0>2\lambda/d+2\), and set
\[
b_T=\lceil C_\beta\log(T\vee2)\rceil,
\]
where the fixed constant \(C_\beta\) is sufficiently large that
\[
T\beta_0\rho_0^{b_T}\le T^{-A_0}.
\tag{16}
\]
Partition \(\{1,\ldots,T\}\) into consecutive blocks of length at most \(b_T\), and split those blocks into odd and even subfamilies.  Blocks in either one subfamily are separated by at least \(b_T\) calendar positions.  The definition of conditional absolute regularity permits replacement of one such block by an independent copy with the same conditional marginal at total-variation cost at most \(\beta_P(b_T\mid E_0)\).  Successive replacement and the triangle inequality therefore couple either parity subfamily to the product of its conditional block marginals with error at most
\[
C(T/b_T)\beta_P(b_T\mid E_0)\le CT^{-A_0}.
\tag{17}
\]

Let \(F\) be either \(\ell_{z,h}\) or \(v^\top\Phi_{z,h}v\) with \(\|v\|_2=1\), and let \(W_g\) be the sum of \(F(X_{st})\) over block \(g\) in one parity.  Boundedness of \(K\) and of \(b_r\) on the support of \(K\) implies
\[
0\le W_g\le Cb_T,
\qquad
W_g^2\le Cb_TW_g.
\]
Under the product law in (17), the variables \(W_g\) are independent.  Equations (14)--(15) imply
\[
\sum_g\operatorname{Var}(W_g)
\le\sum_g\mathbb E[W_g^2]
\le Cb_TTh^d.
\tag{18}
\]
For \(V_g=W_g-\mathbb EW_g\), expansion of the exponential series, together with \(|V_g|\le Cb_T\), gives for \(0<\theta<(Cb_T)^{-1}\)
\[
\mathbb E e^{\theta V_g}
\le\exp\left\{
\frac{\theta^2\operatorname{Var}(W_g)}{2(1-C\theta b_T)}
\right\}.
\tag{19}
\]
Multiplying (19), applying the exponential Markov inequality, and optimizing \(\theta\) for a deviation proportional to \(Th^d\) yields
\[
P\left\{
\left|\sum_g(W_g-\mathbb EW_g)\right|>cTh^d
\right\}
\le C\exp\left(-c\frac{Th^d}{b_T}\right).
\tag{20}
\]
Apply (20) to both parity families and add the coupling error (17).

For the Gram matrix, apply the resulting scalar bound to \(v^\top\Phi_{z,h}v\) over a fixed \(1/4\)-net \(\mathcal V\) of the unit sphere.  Its cardinality is fixed because \(q_r\) is fixed.  For every symmetric matrix \(A\), approximation of a maximizing eigenvector by an element of \(\mathcal V\) gives
\[
\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}
\le2\max_{v\in\mathcal V}|v^\top Av|.
\tag{21}
\]
Equations (14)--(21) show that, outside an event of probability at most
\[
C\exp\left(-c\frac{Th^d}{b_T}\right)+CT^{-A_0},
\tag{22}
\]
the calendar-level mass is at most \(2C_0Th^d\), whereas the calendar-level Gram matrix is at least \((c_0/2)Th^dI_{q_r}\).  Replication multiplies both by \(n_s\):
\[
L_s(h)=n_s\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell_{z,h}(X_{st}),
\qquad
G_s(h)=n_s\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Phi_{z,h}(X_{st}).
\tag{23}
\]
The candidate therefore passes the normalized-shape test outside (22), and
\[
P\left\{L_s(h)=0\ \text{or}\
\lambda_{\min}\left(\frac{G_s(h)}{L_s(h)}\right)<c_G
\,\middle|\,E_0,\widetilde z_s\right\}
\le C\exp\left(-c\frac{Th^d}{b_T}\right)+CT^{-A_0}.
\tag{24}
\]
No response variable and no upper-local-mass event occurs in (24).

Write \(h_0=h_{s,\beta}\).  If \(h_0<1\), its definition and a sufficiently large fixed \(C_h\) give
\[
\frac{T(2^vh_0)^d}{b_T}\ge c2^{vd}
\tag{25}
\]
for every dyadic candidate \(2^vh_0\le1\).  If selection has not stopped by that candidate, the candidate has failed.  Substitution of (25) into (24) proves
\[
P\{h_s>2^vh_{s,\beta}\mid E_0,\widetilde z_s\}
\le C\exp(-c2^{vd})+CT^{-A_0}.
\tag{26}
\]
When \(h_0=1\), this assertion is immediate.  At the terminal candidate \(h=1\), (24) gives
\[
P\{\text{terminal-grid failure}\mid E_0,\widetilde z_s\}
\le C\exp\{-cT/\log(T\vee2)\}+CT^{-A_0}.
\tag{27}
\]

Fix \(a>0\).  In (16) the auxiliary coupling-block constant can be enlarged so that the polynomial remainder is \(T^{-A_a}\) for any fixed \(A_a>a/d+2\); this changes only the proof coupling and not the estimator.  The dyadic tail sum and (26) then yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_P[h_s^a\mathbf1_{\mathrm{good}}\mid E_0,\widetilde z_s]
&\le h_0^a+
\sum_{v:\,2^vh_0<1}(2^{v+1}h_0)^a
P\{h_s>2^vh_0\mid E_0,\widetilde z_s\}\\
&\le Ch_0^a+CT^{-A_a}\\
&\le C\left\{(Tn_s)^{-a/(2\lambda+d)}
+\left(\frac{\log(T\vee2)}T\right)^{a/d}
+N^{-a/2}\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{28}
\]
Here \(\sum_{v\ge0}2^{av}e^{-c2^{vd}}<\infty\), and the grid is capped at one.

There is one selected fit per cohort.  A union bound over fixed \(S\) in (27) controls all selector failures.  The donor fourth-moment assumption makes \(\bar Z\) and its projection finite almost surely; a successful normalized Gram matrix is invertible; and \(M_4(N)\), \(q_N\), and \(\delta_N\) are finite for every positive \(N\).  Since fixed \(D\) and \(\alpha_{\mathrm{don}}>0\) imply \(q_N\le C\), one has \(\delta_N\le CN^{-1/2}\), so \(\delta_N\le\delta_0\) eventually.  For the finitely many earlier indices, the deterministic bad-event indicator is bounded by a constant multiple of \(R_{\mathrm{don}}\).  Moreover, since \(A_0>2\lambda/d+2\),
\[
e^{-cT/\log(T\vee2)}+T^{-A_0}
\le C\left\{\frac{\log(T\vee2)}T\right\}^{2\lambda/d}
=CR_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}.
\tag{29}
\]
Thus \(P(\mathrm{bad}\mid E_0)\le CR_{\star,\beta}\) along every stated array.  Finally, directly from the maximum defining the initial scale,
\[
T\{(Tn_s)^{-1/(2\lambda+d)}\}^d
\quad\text{may be }O(1),
\qquad
Th_{s,\beta}^d\ge c\log(T\vee2).
\tag{30}
\]
The second relation, rather than a dense-local-site hypothesis, supplies (25).  This proves the claim using geometric mixing of the design alone.

Write \(a=a_{\mathrm w}\).  We construct all unspecified variables on one probability space conditional on \(E_0\), using design and donor laws that do not depend on \(\rho\in\mathcal R\).  Fix the displayed \(z_0\in\mathcal Z_+\cap[\delta_0,1-\delta_0]^d\), and let \(E_0\) be degenerate at an event state having this realized path.  Independently over \(t=1,\ldots,T\), draw \(X_{1t}\) uniformly on \([0,1]^d\).  Conditional on the complete design, independently over \((t,i)\), draw
\[
 P_\rho(U_{1ti}=u,V_{1ti}=v\mid X_{1t}=x,E_0)
 =\frac{1+\rho(x)uv}{4},
 \qquad (u,v)\in\{-1,1\}^2.
\]
The defining bound \(\sup_x|\rho(x)|\le 1-2\delta_0\) for \(\mathcal R\) gives
\[
 \frac{1+\rho(x)uv}{4}
 \ge \frac{1-|\rho(x)|}{4}
 \ge\frac{\delta_0}{2}>0,
 \qquad
 \sum_{u,v\in\{-1,1\}}\frac{1+\rho(x)uv}{4}=1.
\]
Thus this is a well-defined conditional law with common support.  Independently over \(i\), draw the event sign pairs from the analogous kernel evaluated at \(x=z_0\), independently of all historical variables given \(E_0\).  Define
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 B_{1i}(0)&=(1+aU_{1i})(1+aV_{1i}),
 &B_{1i}(1)&=B_{1i}^{\mathrm{obs}}=1,\\
 Q_{1ti}(0)&=Q_{1ti}(1)=Q_{1ti}
 & &=(1+aU_{1ti})(1+aV_{1ti}).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Set \(W_{1i,-1}=1\), \(R_{1i0}(0)=aU_{1i}\), \(R_{1i1}(0)=aV_{1i}\), and \(R_{1ih}(1)=0\) for \(h=0,1\).  Since \(-a>-1\), the stipulated return support holds, and \texttt{def:buyhold-level} gives exactly the displayed values of \(B_{1i}(0)\) and \(B_{1i}(1)\).  For every assignment vector, set \(B_{1i}(b,\mathbf a_{-1i})=B_{1i}(b)\) for \(b\in\{0,1\}\).  These constructions verify, respectively, \texttt{ass:consistency}, \texttt{ass:historical-consistency}, \texttt{ass:no-spillovers}, and \texttt{ass:limited-anticipation}.

We next complete the donor law using its full stacked covariance.  Here \(S=1\), so \(Sd=d\).  Conditional on \(E_0\), let \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N\) be independent and uniform on the Euclidean sphere of radius \(\sqrt d\) in \(\mathbb R^d\), independent of the design, historical outcomes, and event outcomes, and put
\[
 Z_j=z_0+\xi_j.
\]
Rotational invariance implies \(\mathbb E(\xi_j\mid E_0)=0\) and \(\mathbb E(\xi_j\xi_j^\top\mid E_0)=cI_d\) for some \(c\).  Taking traces and using \(\|\xi_j\|_2^2=d\) gives \(cd=d\), hence \(c=1\).  Therefore
\[
 \mathbb E(Z_j\mid E_0)=z_0,
 \qquad
 \Sigma=\operatorname{Var}(Z_j\mid E_0)=I_d.
\]
Because \(c_\Sigma\le1\le C_\Sigma\), the full-matrix inequality
\[
 c_\Sigma I_d\preceq\Sigma\preceq C_\Sigma I_d
\]
follows.  Moreover, the premise \(B\ge d^2\) yields
\[
 \mathbb E_{P_\rho}\!\left[
   \left\|\Sigma^{-1/2}(Z_j-z_0)\right\|_2^4
   \,\middle|\,E_0
 \right]
 =\mathbb E(\|\xi_j\|_2^4\mid E_0)
 =d^2\le B.
\]
Thus \texttt{ass:donor-replication}, \texttt{ass:donor-independence}, \texttt{ass:donor-ellipticity}, and \texttt{ass:donor-fourth-moment} all hold; in particular, the construction uses the stipulated full covariance rather than coordinatewise variance surrogates.

Summing the four-point kernel gives, for every \(x\in[0,1]^d\),
\[
 \mathbb E_{P_\rho}(U_{1ti}\mid X_{1t}=x,E_0)
 =\mathbb E_{P_\rho}(V_{1ti}\mid X_{1t}=x,E_0)=0,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_{P_\rho}(U_{1ti}V_{1ti}\mid X_{1t}=x,E_0)=\rho(x).
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E_{P_\rho}[Q_{1ti}\mid X_{1t}=x,E_0]
 &=\mathbb E_{P_\rho}[(1+aU_{1ti})(1+aV_{1ti})
       \mid X_{1t}=x,E_0]\\
 &=1+a\mathbb E(U_{1ti}\mid X_{1t}=x,E_0)
     +a\mathbb E(V_{1ti}\mid X_{1t}=x,E_0)\\
 &\qquad
     +a^2\mathbb E(U_{1ti}V_{1ti}\mid X_{1t}=x,E_0)\\
 &=1+a^2\rho(x).
 \end{aligned}
\]
It follows that \(m_1^{P_\rho}(x)=1+a^2\rho(x)\), which verifies \texttt{ass:historical-regression}; the displayed premise \(\{1+a^2\rho:\rho\in\mathcal R\}\subset\mathcal H_d(\lambda,L)\) verifies \texttt{ass:holder-smoothness}.  Since \(H=1\) and \(p\ge1\), the definition \(d=p(H+1)\) gives \(d=2p\ge2\).  Hence
\[
 0<(1-a)^2\le Q_{1ti},B_{1i}(0)
 \le(1+a)^2<4\le d^2\le B,
 \qquad 0\le B_{1i}(1)=1\le B.
\]
This verifies \texttt{ass:bounded-historical-wealth} and \texttt{ass:bounded-event-wealth}.

The proposition's variance premise also makes the historical response nondegenerate, although such a lower bound is not a member condition of \(\mathcal M_{N,T,(n_1)}(\lambda)\).  Given \(X_{1t}=x\), abbreviate \(U=U_{1ti}\), \(V=V_{1ti}\), and \(r=\rho(x)\).  The kernel identities
\[
 \mathbb E(U+V)=0,
 \quad \mathbb E(UV)=r,
 \quad (U+V)^2=2+2UV,
 \quad (U+V)UV=U+V
\]
give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Var}_{P_\rho}(Q_{1ti}\mid X_{1t}=x,E_0)
 &=\operatorname{Var}\{a(U+V)+a^2UV\mid X_{1t}=x,E_0\}\\
 &=a^2\mathbb E\{(U+V)^2\mid X_{1t}=x,E_0\}
   +a^4\operatorname{Var}(UV\mid X_{1t}=x,E_0)\\
 &\qquad+2a^3\mathbb E\{(U+V)(UV-r)\mid X_{1t}=x,E_0\}\\
 &=2a^2(1+r)+a^4(1-r^2)\ge B^{-1}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Indeed, the cross term is zero because \(\mathbb E\{(U+V)UV\}=\mathbb E(U+V)=0\).  This is a derived property of the witness, not an additional assumption.

The uniform design has density one.  Since \(c_X\le1\le C_X\), this proves \texttt{ass:design-density}.  Conditional on the complete design and \(E_0\), the outcome paths and event outcomes were drawn independently across distinct units, proving \texttt{ass:cross-unit-independence}.  The identical kernels selected for this witness are an admissible special case of the heterogeneous bounded unit laws allowed by the class; no equality in distribution across units is invoked for class membership.  The design sequence \((X_{1t})_{t=1}^T\) is conditionally independent, so its design-only absolute-regularity coefficient satisfies
\[
 \beta_{P_\rho}(\ell_{\mathrm{mix}}\mid E_0)=0
 \le\beta_0\rho_0^{\ell_{\mathrm{mix}}},
 \qquad \ell_{\mathrm{mix}}\ge1,
\]
which is \texttt{ass:temporal-mixing}.  Setting \(X_{1t}^{\mathrm{obs}}=X_{1t}\) verifies \texttt{ass:exact-training-coordinates}.  The stipulated location of \(z_0\) implies
\[
 \operatorname{dist}(z_0,\partial[0,1]^d)\ge\delta_0,
\]
and hence verifies \texttt{ass:interior-event-path}.  Because the event state is degenerate at the displayed admissible path,
\[
 P_\rho\{z_0\in\mathcal Z_+\}=1\ge c_X,
\]
which proves \texttt{ass:positive-query-region}.

It remains to verify the modulus and event transport.  Since \(S=1\), the weight restriction \(\sum_{s=1}^S\pi_s=1\) gives \(\pi_1=1\), and \(\Sigma=I_d\).  Therefore \texttt{def:local-modulus} and the regression formula above yield
\[
 \omega_{P_\rho}(\delta;z_0)
 =a^2\sup_{\substack{\|u\|_2\le\delta\\ z_0+u\in[0,1]^d}}
       |\rho(z_0+u)-\rho(z_0)|.
\]
By the defining property of \(\mathcal R\), the induced surface \(x\mapsto1+a^2\rho(x)\) satisfies the maintained two-sided covariance-standardized local-modulus bounds.  Thus
\[
 c_{\mathrm{mod}}\delta^\kappa
 \le\omega_{P_\rho}(\delta;z_0)
 \le C_{\mathrm{mod}}\delta^\kappa,
 \qquad 0<\delta\le\delta_0,
\]
with \(\kappa=\min\{\lambda,1\}\), verifying \texttt{ass:local-two-sided-modulus}.  The untreated event pair uses the same kernel at \(z_0\).  Repeating the preceding conditional-mean calculation at that point gives
\[
 \mathbb E_{P_\rho}[B_{1i}(0)\mid z_0,E_0]
 =1+a^2\rho(z_0)=m_1^{P_\rho}(z_0).
\]
Averaging this equality over \(i=1,\ldots,n_1\) proves \texttt{ass:event-transport}.  We have now verified every member property in \texttt{def:panel-law-class}, and hence
\[
 \{P_\rho:\rho\in\mathcal R\}
 \subset\mathcal M_{N,T,(n_1)}(\lambda).
\]
The indexing family is nonempty and relatively open by the definition of \(\mathcal R\).

We next derive the causal target, keeping it distinct from the observed-law regression.  By \texttt{def:target}, the potential-outcome construction, and the event-transport equality just proved,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \tau_{n,P_\rho}(z_0)
 &=\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}
   \mathbb E_{P_\rho}[B_{1i}(1)-B_{1i}(0)\mid z_0,E_0]\\
 &=1-\{1+a^2\rho(z_0)\}\\
 &=-a^2\rho(z_0).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus the equality between the causal contrast and the regression surface is a consequence of event transport, not a definition of the causal estimand.

Finally, marginalizing the sign kernel gives, for \(u,v\in\{-1,1\}\),
\[
 P_\rho(U=u\mid x,E_0)
 =\sum_{v'\in\{-1,1\}}\frac{1+\rho(x)uv'}4=\frac12,
 \qquad
 P_\rho(V=v\mid x,E_0)=\frac12.
\]
Hence each untreated return coordinate has the common symmetric two-point conditional law on \(\{-a,a\}\), and in particular conditional mean zero, for every \(\rho\).  Every treated return coordinate is identically zero.  The initial-wealth law is the common point mass at one, and \(\mathbb E_{P_\rho}[B_{1i}(1)\mid z_0,E_0]=1\).  It follows from \texttt{def:mean-only-information} that \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{mean}}(P_\rho)\) is constant over \(\rho\in\mathcal R\).

To obtain a separated pair, choose \(\rho_*\in\mathcal R\).  Relative openness in the H\"older ball gives \(\epsilon>0\) such that
\[
 \{g\in\mathcal H_d(\lambda,L):
       \|g-\rho_*\|_{\mathcal H_d}<\epsilon\}
 \subset\mathcal R.
\]
Choose a constant function \(c\in\mathcal H_d(\lambda,L)\) with \(c\ne\rho_*(z_0)\), which is possible because \(L>0\).  For \(0<\eta<1\), define \(\rho_\eta=(1-\eta)\rho_*+\eta c\).  The H\"older ball is convex: each seminorm and the supremum norm of \(\rho_\eta\) is bounded by the same convex combination of the corresponding bounds for \(\rho_*\) and \(c\).  Thus \(\rho_\eta\in\mathcal H_d(\lambda,L)\), and
\[
 \|\rho_\eta-\rho_*\|_{\mathcal H_d}
 =\eta\|c-\rho_*\|_{\mathcal H_d}<\epsilon
\]
for all sufficiently small \(\eta>0\).  It follows that \(\rho_\eta\in\mathcal R\), while
\[
 \rho_\eta(z_0)-\rho_*(z_0)
 =\eta\{c-\rho_*(z_0)\}\ne0.
\]
Set \(\rho^{(0)}=\rho_*\) and \(\rho^{(1)}=\rho_\eta\).  Constancy of the restricted information map and the causal-target formula imply
\[
 \mathcal O_{\mathrm{mean}}(P_{\rho^{(0)}})
 =\mathcal O_{\mathrm{mean}}(P_{\rho^{(1)}}),
\]
but
\[
 \left|\tau_{n,P_{\rho^{(1)}}}(z_0)
       -\tau_{n,P_{\rho^{(0)}}}(z_0)\right|
 =a^2\left|\rho^{(1)}(z_0)-\rho^{(0)}(z_0)\right|>0.
\]
If \(\tau_n\) were a functional of \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{mean}}\), equal information maps would force equal target values, contradicting the last display.  The full historical wealth laws need not coincide because the conditional joint sign law, and generally the conditional law of \(Q_{1ti}\), varies with \(\rho\).  The conclusion is therefore precisely nonidentification from the restricted mean-only map, not observational equivalence under the maintained full historical wealth panel.

Set
\[
a:=\frac{2\lambda}{2\lambda+d}
\quad\text{and}\quad
q:=\frac{2\lambda}{d}.
\]
Because \(\lambda>0\) and \(d>0\), one has \(a\in(0,1)\) and \(q>0\).  We first prove the weighted geometric--arithmetic mean inequality needed below.  For \(u>0\), let
\[
\phi(u):=au+(1-a)-u^a.
\]
Then \(\phi(1)=0\), and differentiation gives
\[
\phi'(u)=a\bigl(1-u^{a-1}\bigr).
\]
Since \(a-1<0\), the derivative is negative on \((0,1)\) and positive on \((1,\infty)\).  Hence \(u=1\) is a global minimizer and \(\phi(u)\geq0\).  Substituting \(u=x/y\) and multiplying by \(y>0\) proves
\[
x^a y^{1-a}\leq ax+(1-a)y,
\qquad x>0,quad y>0.
\]

The definitions of \(a\) and \(q\) imply
\[
q(1-a)
=\frac{2\lambda}{d}\frac{d}{2\lambda+d}
=\frac{2\lambda}{2\lambda+d}
=a.
\]
For each cohort \(s\), positivity of the integers \(T\) and \(n_s\) therefore permits the preceding inequality with \(x=n_s^{-1}\) and \(y=T^{-q}\).  It yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
(Tn_s)^{-2\lambda/(2\lambda+d)}
&=n_s^{-a}T^{-a}\\
&=(n_s^{-1})^a(T^{-q})^{1-a}\\
&\leq a n_s^{-1}+(1-a)T^{-q}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The cohort weights in \(\texttt{def:rate-frontier}\) are positive and satisfy \(\sum_{s=1}^S\pi_s=1\), so
\[
\sum_{s=1}^S\pi_s^2
\leq\left(\sum_{s=1}^S\pi_s\right)^2
=1.
\]
Multiplying the cohortwise inequality by \(\pi_s^2\), summing over \(s\), and invoking the definitions of \(R_{\mathrm{sm}}\) and \(R_{\mathrm{tr}}\) gives
\[
R_{\mathrm{sm}}
\leq aR_{\mathrm{tr}}+(1-a)T^{-q}.
\tag{1}
\]

For every positive integer \(T\),
\(\log(T\vee2)\geq\log2>0\).  Thus the definition of \(R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}\) in \(\texttt{def:rate-frontier}\) gives
\[
T^{-q}
\leq(\log2)^{-q}
\left\{\frac{\log(T\vee2)}{T}\right\}^{q}
=(\log2)^{-q}R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}.
\tag{2}
\]
Combining \((1)\) and \((2)\), and using the elementary inequality \(cx+dy\leq(c+d)(x\vee y)\) for nonnegative \(c,d,x,y\), proves
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_{\mathrm{sm}}
&\leq aR_{\mathrm{tr}}+(1-a)(\log2)^{-q}R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}\\
&\leq\bigl\{a+(1-a)(\log2)^{-q}\bigr\}
\bigl(R_{\mathrm{tr}}\vee R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}\bigr)\\
&=C_{\lambda,d}
\bigl(R_{\mathrm{tr}}\vee R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}\bigr),
\end{aligned}
\]
where the last equality follows from \(1-a=d/(2\lambda+d)\) and \(q=2\lambda/d\).  Moreover, \(0<\log2<1\), so \((\log2)^{-q}>1\) and consequently \(C_{\lambda,d}\geq a+(1-a)=1\).

Let
\[
A:=R_{\mathrm{tr}}\vee R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}
\quad\text{and}\quad
D_0:=A\vee R_{\mathrm{don}}.
\]
All these quantities are positive by \(\texttt{def:rate-frontier}\).  Its definition of \(R_{\star,\beta}\), the preceding bound, and \(C_{\lambda,d}\geq1\) imply
\[
D_0
\leq R_{\star,\beta}
=D_0\vee R_{\mathrm{sm}}
\leq D_0\vee(C_{\lambda,d}A)
\leq C_{\lambda,d}D_0.
\]
This proves
\[
R_{\star,\beta}
\asymp_{\lambda,d}
R_{\mathrm{tr}}\vee R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}\vee R_{\mathrm{don}},
\]
with comparison constants \(1\) and \(C_{\lambda,d}\), which do not depend on \(N,T,S\), or the positive replication counts.

Now let \(T\geq3\).  Then \(T\vee2=T\) and \(\log T\geq1\), so
\[
T^{-q}
\leq\left(\frac{\log T}{T}\right)^q
=R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}.
\]
Substitution into \((1)\) gives
\[
R_{\mathrm{sm}}
\leq aR_{\mathrm{tr}}+(1-a)R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}
\leq R_{\mathrm{tr}}\vee R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta},
\]
where the second inequality follows from \(a\in(0,1)\).  Taking the maximum with the remaining rate components in \(\texttt{def:rate-frontier}\) now yields the exact identity
\[
R_{\star,\beta}
=R_{\mathrm{tr}}\vee R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}\vee R_{\mathrm{don}}.
\]

By \(\texttt{def:rate-frontier}\), \(R_{\mathrm{don}}=N^{-\kappa}\).  Along any joint growth array, this channel is negligible relative to \(A\) precisely when
\[
N^{-\kappa}=o(A),
\]
whereas it dominates \(A\) precisely when
\[
A=o(N^{-\kappa}).
\]
Because \(\kappa>0\), the boundary relation \(N^{-\kappa}\asymp A\) is equivalent, after applying the decreasing map \(x\mapsto x^{-1/\kappa}\) and absorbing the fixed comparison constants, to
\[
N\asymp A^{-1/\kappa}.
\]
These comparisons describe minimax phases only in an experiment for which a separate statistical result establishes \(R_{\star,\beta}\) as the sharp risk; none of the preceding algebra asserts that statistical premise.

For the independent-design comparator, or under the separately imposed fixed-query local-small-ball/anti-clustering condition specified in \(\texttt{def:rate-frontier}\), the delivered spacing component is
\[
R_{\mathrm{sp}}=T^{-q}.
\]
Equation \((1)\) then becomes
\[
R_{\mathrm{sm}}
\leq aR_{\mathrm{tr}}+(1-a)R_{\mathrm{sp}}
\leq R_{\mathrm{tr}}\vee R_{\mathrm{sp}}.
\]
The comparator definition of \(R_\star\) consequently gives
\[
R_\star
=R_{\mathrm{tr}}\vee R_{\mathrm{sm}}\vee R_{\mathrm{sp}}\vee R_{\mathrm{don}}
=R_{\mathrm{tr}}\vee R_{\mathrm{sp}}\vee R_{\mathrm{don}}.
\]

Finally, \(\texttt{ass:exact-training-coordinates}\) states
\[
X_{st}^{\mathrm{obs}}=X_{st}.
\]
Thus the historical design coordinate used by a regression functional is observed without a measurement-error convolution, so no inversion of such a convolution is required.  Consistently, the exhaustive maximum defining \(R_{\star,\beta}\) in \(\texttt{def:rate-frontier}\) contains neither a deconvolution component nor a separate moving-Gram component.  The same definition uses \(\kappa=\min\{\lambda,1\}\).  If \(\lambda>1\), then \(\kappa=1\), and hence
\[
R_{\mathrm{don}}=N^{-\kappa}=N^{-1}.
\]
All assertions follow.

It is enough to construct one admissible triangular array.  Fix
\[
H=0,\qquad p=S=d=1,\qquad \lambda=\kappa=1,\qquad \pi_1=1,
\]
and choose
\[
B=16,\qquad c_X=C_X=c_\Sigma=C_\Sigma=1,
\qquad \delta_0=\frac14,\qquad
c_{\mathrm{mod}}=C_{\mathrm{mod}}=1.
\]
Choose any admissible positive geometric-mixing constants \(\beta_0\) and
\(\rho_0\), take the H\"older radius \(L\) large enough to contain the affine
function introduced below, let
\(K(u)=\mathbf 1\{|u|\leq 1\}\), and choose the normalized-shape threshold
so that \(0<c_G\leq1\).  The prescribed polynomial degree and basis are then
\[
r=\lceil1\rceil-1=0,\qquad b_0(u)=e_0=1.
\]
Let \(E_0\) be constant, put \(z_0=1/2\), set
\(\mathcal Z_+=\{1/2\}\), and, for every positive integer \(T\), set
\[
n_1=N=T^2.
\]

We first define the historical experiment and verify its restrictions.  Write
\(X_t=X_{1t}\), and let \(X_1,\ldots,X_T\) be independent uniform random
variables on \([0,1]\).  Define
\[
m(x)=8+x-\frac12,
\qquad
Q_{1ti}=m(X_t)+\frac12U_{ti},
\]
where the variables \((U_{ti})_{t,i}\) are mutually independent Rademacher
variables and are independent of the complete design.  Since
\(m([0,1])=[15/2,17/2]\),
\[
7\leq Q_{1ti}\leq9\leq B,
\qquad
\mathbb E_P[Q_{1ti}\mid X_t=x,E_0]=m(x).
\]
Thus \texttt{ass:bounded-historical-wealth} and
\texttt{ass:historical-regression} hold for every replicated unit.  The affine
function \(m\) belongs to \(\mathcal H_1(1,L)\) by the choice of \(L\), so
\texttt{ass:holder-smoothness} holds.  The conditional design density is one,
which verifies \texttt{ass:design-density} with the displayed constants.  The
design process is independent over calendar time; hence, for the design-mixing
lag \(\ell_{\mathrm{mix}}\),
\[
\beta_P(\ell_{\mathrm{mix}}\mid E_0)=0
\leq\beta_0\rho_0^{\ell_{\mathrm{mix}}}
\qquad(\ell_{\mathrm{mix}}\geq1),
\]
which is \texttt{ass:temporal-mixing}.  Finally set
\(X_{1t}^{\mathrm{obs}}=X_t\); this is
\texttt{ass:exact-training-coordinates}.

Independently of the historical sample, let
\[
Z_j=\frac12+V_j,
\]
where \(V_1,\ldots,V_N\) are independent Rademacher variables.  Therefore
\[
\mathbb E_P[Z_j\mid E_0]=z_0,\qquad
\Sigma=\operatorname{Var}_P(Z_j\mid E_0)=1,
\qquad
\mathbb E_P\!\left[
 |\Sigma^{-1/2}(Z_j-z_0)|^4\mid E_0
\right]=1\leq B.
\]
These equalities verify, respectively, the defining relation for \(z_0\),
\texttt{ass:donor-ellipticity}, and
\texttt{ass:donor-fourth-moment}; the construction also gives
\texttt{ass:donor-replication} and \texttt{ass:donor-independence}.
For \(0<\delta\leq\delta_0\), every \(z_0+u\) with \(|u|\leq\delta\)
lies in \([0,1]\).  Consequently \texttt{def:local-modulus} gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\omega_P(\delta;z_0)
&=\sup_{|u|\leq\delta}|m(z_0+u)-m(z_0)|\\
&=\sup_{|u|\leq\delta}|u|=\delta.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves \texttt{ass:local-two-sided-modulus} with
\(c_{\mathrm{mod}}=C_{\mathrm{mod}}=1\).  Also
\[
\operatorname{dist}(z_0,\partial[0,1])=\frac12\geq\delta_0,
\qquad
P\{z_0\in\mathcal Z_+\}=1\geq c_X,
\]
so \texttt{ass:interior-event-path} and
\texttt{ass:positive-query-region} hold.

It remains to specify the causal variables.  Define the design-measurable
event shock
\[
\Gamma=\mathbf 1\{X_1\leq1/4\}
\]
and set, for every \(i\),
\[
B_{1i}(0)=8,\qquad B_{1i}(1)=8+\Gamma,
\qquad B_{1i}^{\mathrm{obs}}=B_{1i}(1).
\]
Define \(B_{1i}(a,\mathbf a_{-1i})=B_{1i}(a)\), and put
\(Q_{1ti}(a)=Q_{1ti}\) for \(a\in\{0,1\}\).  These definitions verify
\texttt{ass:consistency}, \texttt{ass:historical-consistency},
\texttt{ass:no-spillovers}, and \texttt{ass:limited-anticipation}.  They also
give \(0\leq B_{1i}(a)\leq9<B\), establishing
\texttt{ass:bounded-event-wealth}.  The construction is compatible with
\texttt{def:buyhold-level}: take
\[
W_{1i,-1}=1,
\qquad
R_{1i0}(a)=B_{1i}(a)-1>-1,
\]
for then \(W_{1i,-1}\{1+R_{1i0}(a)\}=B_{1i}(a)\).
Since \(m(z_0)=8\),
\[
\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}
\mathbb E_P[B_{1i}(0)\mid z_0,E_0]
=8=m(z_0),
\]
which is exactly \texttt{ass:event-transport}.  Conditional on the complete
design and \(E_0\), every event outcome is constant and the historical path
of unit \(i\) is a measurable function of
\((U_{ti})_{t=1}^T\).  Independence of these vectors across \(i\) therefore
proves \texttt{ass:cross-unit-independence}.  We have now checked every member
property in \texttt{def:panel-law-class}, and hence the resulting law \(P_T\)
belongs to \(\mathcal M_{N,T,\mathbf n}(1)\).

Because \(z_0\) and \(E_0\) are constant and the uniform design gives
\(P(\Gamma=1)=1/4\), \texttt{def:target} yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\tau_n(z_0)
&=\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}
  \mathbb E_P[B_{1i}(1)-B_{1i}(0)\mid z_0,E_0]\\
&=\mathbb E_P[\Gamma]=\frac14,
\qquad
\bar B_1^{\mathrm{obs}}=8+\Gamma.
\end{aligned}
\]
This calculation keeps the causal target distinct from the random observed
event mean.

We next evaluate the estimator in \texttt{def:feasible-estimator}.  Its
generated center is
\[
\bar Z=\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N Z_j,
\qquad
\widetilde z=\Pi_{[0,1]}(\bar Z).
\]
Projection onto \([0,1]\) fixes \(z_0\) and cannot increase scalar distance
from \(z_0\).  Using independence and
\(\mathbb E[V_j]=0\), \(\mathbb E[V_j^2]=1\), we obtain
\[
|\widetilde z-z_0|
\leq\left|\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^NV_j\right|,
\qquad
\mathbb E_P[(\widetilde z-z_0)^2\mid E_0]
\leq\frac1{N}=T^{-2}.
\]
For all sufficiently large \(T\), the initial bandwidth is less than one and,
because \(n_1=N=T^2\) and \(T\geq3\), equals
\[
\underline h_T
=C_h\left[(Tn_1)^{-1/3}
\vee\frac{\log(T\vee2)}T\vee N^{-1/2}\right]
=C_h\frac{\log T}{T}.
\]
Define
\[
I_T=\{t:|X_t-\widetilde z|\leq\underline h_T\},
\qquad
\mathcal A_T=\{|I_T|>0\}.
\]
For every fixed \(\widetilde z\in[0,1]\), the intersection of
\([\widetilde z-\underline h_T,\widetilde z+\underline h_T]\) with
\([0,1]\) has Lebesgue measure at least \(\underline h_T\).  Donor
independence and the independent uniform design therefore imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(\mathcal A_T^c\mid E_0,\widetilde z)
&\leq(1-\underline h_T)^T\\
&\leq\exp(-T\underline h_T)=T^{-C_h}.
\end{aligned}
\]
In particular, \(P(\mathcal A_T^c\mid E_0)\to0\).

On \(\mathcal A_T\), the local mass and order-zero Gram matrix at the first
candidate satisfy
\[
L_1=n_1|I_T|,\qquad G_1=n_1|I_T|,
\qquad \lambda_{\min}(G_1/L_1)=1\geq c_G.
\]
Thus the normalized-shape selector accepts the initial candidate, and the
least-squares intercept is
\[
\widehat m_1
=\frac1{n_1|I_T|}
  \sum_{t\in I_T}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}Q_{1ti}.
\]
On this event, its conditional-mean component differs from \(m(z_0)=8\) by
at most
\[
\frac1{|I_T|}\sum_{t\in I_T}|m(X_t)-m(z_0)|
\leq\underline h_T+|\widetilde z-z_0|.
\]
Conditional on the design and donors, its Rademacher component has mean zero
and variance
\[
\operatorname{Var}_P\!\left(
\frac1{2n_1|I_T|}\sum_{t\in I_T}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}U_{ti}
\,\middle|\,(X_t)_{t=1}^T,E_0,(Z_j)_{j=1}^N
\right)
=\frac1{4n_1|I_T|}\leq\frac1{4n_1}.
\]
At every successful order-zero candidate the fitted intercept is an average
of responses in \([7,9]\), while the failed-fit convention sets it to zero.
Thus \((\widehat m_1-8)^2\leq64\) on \(\mathcal A_T^c\), whether a later
candidate succeeds or every candidate fails.  Consequently, for a fixed
constant \(C\), the preceding three displays give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_P[(\widehat m_1-8)^2\mid E_0]
&\leq C\left\{
\underline h_T^2+N^{-1}+n_1^{-1}
+P(\mathcal A_T^c\mid E_0)
\right\}\\
&\longrightarrow0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Denote \(D_T=\widehat m_1-m(z_0)\).  From the displayed target calculation
and the definition of \(\widehat\tau\),
\[
\widehat\tau-\tau_n(z_0)
=\Gamma-\frac14-D_T.
\]
Expanding the square and applying the elementary inequality
\(|\mathbb E[UV]|\leq\{\mathbb E[U^2]\mathbb E[V^2]\}^{1/2}\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left|
\mathbb E_P[(\widehat\tau-\tau_n(z_0))^2\mid E_0]
-\mathbb E_P[(\Gamma-1/4)^2\mid E_0]
\right|\\
&\qquad\leq
2\{\mathbb E_P[(\Gamma-1/4)^2\mid E_0]\}^{1/2}
 \{\mathbb E_P[D_T^2\mid E_0]\}^{1/2}
+\mathbb E_P[D_T^2\mid E_0]
\longrightarrow0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(\Gamma\) is Bernoulli with success probability \(1/4\), it follows
that
\[
\lim_{T\to\infty}
\mathbb E_P\!\left[(\widehat\tau-\tau_n(z_0))^2\mid E_0\right]
=\operatorname{Var}_P(\Gamma)
=\frac14\left(1-\frac14\right)=\frac3{16}.
\]

The four iid-comparator components in \texttt{def:rate-frontier} are
\[
R_{\mathrm{tr}}=n_1^{-1}=T^{-2},
\qquad
R_{\mathrm{sm}}=(Tn_1)^{-2/3}=T^{-2},
\]
\[
R_{\mathrm{sp}}=T^{-2},
\qquad
R_{\mathrm{don}}=N^{-1}=T^{-2}.
\]
Therefore \(R_\star=T^{-2}\), as claimed.

Finally consider the interval in \texttt{def:honest-interval}.  On
\(\mathcal A_T\), the successful local-constant weights are
\[
a_{1ti}=\frac{\mathbf 1\{t\in I_T\}}{n_1|I_T|},
\qquad
\sum_{t=1}^T|a_{1ti}|=\frac1{n_1},
\qquad
\sum_{t=1}^T\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}|a_{1ti}|=1.
\]
For each fixed \(\alpha\in(0,1/2)\), the definitions of the two Hoeffding
radii thus give
\[
R_{\mathrm{hist}}
=B\left\{\frac12\log\left(\frac2{\alpha_{\mathrm{hist}}}\right)
\frac1{n_1}\right\}^{1/2}=O(T^{-1}),
\]
\[
R_{\mathrm{evt}}
=B\left\{\frac12\log\left(\frac2{\alpha_{\mathrm{evt}}}\right)
\frac1{n_1}\right\}^{1/2}=O(T^{-1}).
\]
Kernel support, nonnegativity of the weights, and their unit total mass imply
the deterministic Taylor allowance bound
\[
A_L
\leq C_{0,1}L\underline h_T
=O\!\left(\frac{\log T}{T}\right).
\]
For the donor allowance, \(D=Sd=1\), so the exact calibration in
\texttt{def:honest-interval} gives
\[
M_4(N)=\frac{16}{N}+3\left(1-\frac1N\right)\leq16,
\qquad
q_N=\{M_4(N)/\alpha_{\mathrm{don}}\}^{1/4}=O(1).
\]
Since \(c_\Sigma=C_\Sigma=1\),
\[
\delta_N=\frac{q_N}{\sqrt N}=O(T^{-1}),
\qquad
A_{\mathrm{don}}=C_{\mathrm{mod}}\delta_N^\kappa=O(T^{-1}).
\]
In particular, \(\delta_N\leq\delta_0\) for all sufficiently large \(T\).
On \(\mathcal A_T\), the selected Gram matrix is positive and every required
weight and radius is finite.  Hence, eventually, the bad-sample event of
\texttt{def:honest-interval} is contained in \(\mathcal A_T^c\), and on
\(\mathcal A_T\)
\[
H_\alpha
=R_{\mathrm{hist}}+R_{\mathrm{evt}}+A_L+A_{\mathrm{don}}
=O\!\left(\frac{\log T}{T}\right)=o(1).
\]
The constant in this bound depends on the fixed \(\alpha\) and fixed class
constants but not on the sample realization.  Thus, for all sufficiently
large \(T\), \(H_\alpha<1/8\) throughout \(\mathcal A_T\).

If the nonfallback interval contains \(\tau_n(z_0)\), then necessarily
\(|\widehat\tau-\tau_n(z_0)|\leq H_\alpha\).  But
\(|\Gamma-1/4|\geq1/4\) almost surely, and on
\(\{|D_T|<1/16\}\) the reverse triangle inequality gives
\[
|\widehat\tau-\tau_n(z_0)|
\geq\frac14-\frac1{16}=\frac3{16}>\frac18.
\]
Since fallback can occur only inside \(\mathcal A_T^c\) eventually, we have
the event inclusion
\[
\{\tau_n(z_0)\in C_\alpha\}
\subseteq
\mathcal A_T^c\cup\{|D_T|\geq1/16\}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
P\{\tau_n(z_0)\in C_\alpha\mid E_0\}
&\leq P(\mathcal A_T^c\mid E_0)
 +P(|D_T|\geq1/16\mid E_0)\\
&\leq P(\mathcal A_T^c\mid E_0)
 +256\,\mathbb E_P[D_T^2\mid E_0]
\longrightarrow0.
\end{aligned}
\]
The last inequality follows directly from
\(\mathbf 1\{|D_T|\geq1/16\}\leq256D_T^2\).  This proves both asserted
